rationale: A wins because it finds more real editorial tension without pretending the announcement is bigger than it is. Its best line, "A keyboard-first tool built for engineers now has to serve people who don't live in keyboard shortcuts," is a proper reported tension; B's version, "A keyboard-first tool built for engineers is now pitching itself to designers," sees the same thing but stuffs it into a customer-story frame that dies without a named customer. B is cleaner than most, but A is more useful to a founder deciding what proof to gather and which desk to approach.
gaps_in_A: "Linear opens the product-management market it spent years refusing to enter" invents motive and history. The update says Linear is expanding beyond engineering; it does not say the company refused this market for years.
"Selling to a second buyer without a sales team" overstates the record. The facts say no enterprise sales team is mentioned, not that Linear has no sales team.
"the competitive set is forced to react" is launch-day theater without evidence. No competitor response was supplied.

"What product managers actually lose when their roadmap lives outside the engineers' tool" is a smart trend angle, but it leans on an unsupplied split-stack pain story and correctly needs a named PM before it should leave the building.
gaps_in_B: "Linear, the engineers' issue tracker" imports a product description not given in the update. Close enough for people who know Linear, still not clean for a blind evidence-bound exercise.
"now wants the whole product org" oversells the supplied facts. PMs, designers, and stakeholder views are not automatically the whole product organization.
"without a sales team" makes the same dangerous leap as A. The record only says no enterprise sales team is mentioned.
"Story type: customer-story" is premature. The angle itself admits it needs "at least one named product or design team"; without that, it is a reported idea, not a customer story.
